current_episode.title: 295 Laura Bonamici - Round Two - Former Global Head of Marketing, Fujitsu

guest.bio_context: Laura Bonamici grew up in Sardinia, Italy, and built a career leading away from home, working in the UK, Germany, and Japan. She spent four years as Global Head of Marketing at Fujitsu, where she led transformation initiatives aligned with the company's midterm plans and the launch of the Uvance digital services portfolio. She is known for her approach to translating speed, precision, and global ambition into local contexts across different cultures.

key_stats: Initial assignment duration: 18 months, later extended to 4 years total
Company midterm plan cycle: 3 years, ending March 2025
First checkpoint: 6 months; second checkpoint: 12 months for assignment review
Uvance digital services portfolio: launched in 2021 with ambitious targets through midterm plan
Fiscal year results: most successful year for Fujitsu published end of April following four years of transformation
context.transcript_excerpt: Welcome back to our latest episode of Japan's Top Business Interviews. I'm your host, Dr. Greg Story, President Dale Cunning, Tokyo Training. My special guest today is Laura Bonamichi, who is the former Global Head of Marketing for Fujitsu and the first person to ever be on this podcast twice. And the reason she's on this podcast twice is because I attended an event at the Italian Chamber where she was a speaker. And she gave such an eloquent and such an interesting encapsulation of her insights and observations from her time in Japan that I asked her, I said, you know, we can't let this gold filter away here. We have to capture this for prosperity. So she very kindly agreed to come and talk basically the same talk she gave to the chamber. We're going to do it live here today. Laura, thank you very much. Of course. Thank you for having me back. Yeah, so we already had a lovely interview previously about your views on leading in Japan, but this is going to be broader. Your insights from your time in Japan, so you have a presentation. So I'll be the audience, so go right ahead and let's hear what you came up with. Sure. So let me take you back. For those of you who don't know me, I grew up in Sardinia, Italy. And as a child, my father would take me mushroom picking on weekends. And we would live at six o'clock sharp, which as a teenager, you can imagine, felt a little bit ambitious, let's say. But what was interesting is that he never cared about how late I stayed out the night before. But he expected me to be there on time, by the door, ready to go in the morning. And that was my first lesson. If you don't deliver on your word, people stop trusting you. And without trust, nothing works. When we arrived in the woods, it wouldn't rush in. I always remember this moment where we would ask me to stop, to squat down and to tune in into the environment. I remember we used to say Sintonizzati in Italian. So the idea was to adjust your vision, to understand the environment around you, the colours, the light, the patterns. and only then we would start looking for mushroom. And that was my second lesson because if you don't understand the context, you don't actually see what's there. Then there was a third lesson. So sometimes I would spot beautiful mushroom right in front of me and I would get really excited. But at the same time, I would ask myself, how could he not see those mushrooms? And I realized that he hadn't missed them at all. He was leaving them for me because he understood something that I didn't at the time. So if the task feels too long, If the progress is too slow, people disengage. And leadership ultimately is about that. It's not about just moving forward. It's about bringing people with you. I actually thought a lot about those lessons since I moved to Japan over the last four years. Because leading transformation here at this particular moment feels much closer to walking through those woods than it does to any corporate or management textbook. It requires discipline, it requires attention to context, and it requires also balancing competing realities at the same time. Because on the ground, what it feels like is not just a single direction of travel, it's very much a set of tensions that you have to hold at the same time. That brings me to my view of leadership, especially when you're leading away from home. So leadership is increasingly an act of translation. And by that, I don't mean language translation, which, of course, here in Japan is quite a significant part of leadership. I mean context translation. I mean the ability to move between worlds, between perspectives, between competing realities, and help people, people in your team, make sense of them. So over the last four years, I found myself repeatedly navigating a number of tensions. So those are the ones that I would like to talk a little bit about today. pending_qa.q: How does a leader build lasting legacy that survives leadership transitions?
pending_qa.r: The most powerful thing you can do is find your people and build legacy around those people, because that is what lasts ultimately. While surface-level changes like structure and processes may revert after you leave, the people you develop carry forward pieces of your legacy. Legacy is not about blueprints or playbooks—it is about the village you build and the people you touch, not just spreadsheets. Those people take what resonates with them and evolve it forward.
